A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LaoBench and provide readable text, tables, figures, and equations. All nine pages of v1 and seventeen pages of v2 were inspected, including v2's Appendices A–J; v1 has no appendix. The substantial expansion does not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Lao-7k model evaluations, human expert scores, and Thinking versus Non-Thinking comparisons in Table 2 and Figures 4–5.

after.justification: v2 retains the Lao-7k results and adds original Lao-500 evaluations, chrF++ scores, annotation and judge agreement measurements, and contamination analyses.

M1.justification: The construction method retains expert-written questions, LLM-based prompt scoring, topic clustering, balanced selection, and expert/agent validation. v2 expands documentation without establishing a changed construction algorithm or model. Its new Arena judging procedure is an evaluation protocol addition.

E1.justification: v1 explicitly evaluates only Lao-7k. v2 additionally evaluates Lao-500, extending actual task coverage to open-ended Lao generation, explanation quality, coherence, and instruction following. Lao-500 was already described in v1, but its empirical evaluation is new; Lao-10k still has no reported model results.

E2.justification: The corresponding Lao-7k comparison retains all fourteen LLM configurations, Random Choice, and human experts in Table 2 of v1 and Table 3 of v2. The new Lao-500 comparisons reuse previously evaluated models; assigning GPT-5-High and Claude-Opus-4.1 baseline roles changes the new evaluation design.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 500-prompt Arena protocol with a fixed GPT-5-High baseline, two judges, swapped answer positions, half-win ties, and cross-judge aggregation. It also adds chrF++ evaluation and reliability-check protocols. Newly disclosed LaoNLP/SacreBLEU and decoding settings do not establish that the retained Lao-7k experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing CoT comparison is retained. New appendices examine annotation agreement, judge sensitivity, human–judge agreement on 50 prompts, ranking stability under an alternative baseline, potential contamination, and knowledge/translation failure modes. These substantially broaden analysis of benchmark and evaluation reliability.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v2 adds prompt-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, judge rank correlations, and Fleiss' kappa for annotation agreement. Appendix J also newly describes three-expert mean/standard-deviation reporting, although Table 3 supplies no standard deviations. These are new reporting practices, not evidence of increased runs for the original experiments.

E6.justification: The numerical Lao-7k results match between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. v2 adds Lao-500 win rates and intervals, chrF++ scores for three models, annotation kappa of 0.87, human–judge agreement of 84%, and potential overlap affecting 6.2% of items. These are additional findings, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 formally defines the new Arena score through tie-adjusted win signals, cross-judge averaging, and a prompt-bootstrap estimator in Equations 1–3. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claim of a first large-scale, multidimensional Lao benchmark is retained. However, v1 claims to establish an official evaluation platform, whereas v2 narrows this contribution to a designed black-box protocol whose online service will be deployed upon publication.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning multiple-choice test-taking strategies, BLEU tokenization/paraphrase sensitivity, judge preferences, and baseline anchoring. It also interprets differences between open-ended and closed-form rankings, cross-judge preference shifts, contamination candidates, and specific error mechanisms. v1 primarily discusses general model weaknesses and CoT benefits.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a dataset access link, detailed counts and taxonomy, annotator/reviewer numbers, annotation rules, LaoNLP version, metric settings, decoding information, exact Arena prompts, parsing rules, and planned black-box submission procedures. However, it removes v1's specific BERTopic, text-embedding-3-small, UMAP, and HDBSCAN implementation disclosures. Documentation changes substantially in both directions.

R1.justification: v2 adds a structured comparison with regional and language-specific benchmarks, including SeaEval, SEA-HELM, SeaExam/SeaBench, VMLU, and LORAXBENCH. Together with new contamination literature, this substantially expands positioning around native construction, cultural and educational coverage, and held-out evaluation. MiLiC-Eval's publication entry represents an existing work, not a new research comparator.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark description, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 4, construction subsections are consolidated, and detailed statistics move into appendices. Dedicated Limitations and Ethics sections and Appendices A–J substantially reorganize the document.

P2.justification: The example and construction diagrams are redrawn and exchange figure numbers. The main results table is restyled and placed alongside the existing aggregate plot. New benchmark-comparison, taxonomy, prompt, and result tables plus an Arena confidence-interval plot substantially expand the displays; the distribution and CoT plots retain their underlying content.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's missing open-ended evaluation and supplies useful reproducibility details and explicit limitations. However, its central new reliability evidence is inconsistent: Appendix D reports judge Spearman/Kendall correlations of 0.83/0.71, while the twelve score pairs in Table 9 yield 0.00/about 0.03. No different correlation sample is specified. This unresolved discrepancy, alongside removed construction details, prevents a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial additions.
